objectives: Use age-based respiratory rate thresholds when assessing cough and difficult breathing.
Screen danger signs before deciding outpatient treatment at HC III.
Classify and manage likely pneumonia using IMNCI and Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023.
takeaways: A child aged 12-59 months with RR 48/min has fast breathing.
No chest indrawing, no stridor at rest, and ability to drink support outpatient pneumonia care.
Caregiver counseling on danger signs and 2-day review is essential.
learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A 2-year-old with cough and fever arrives at a busy HC III. Decide whether this is routine cough, pneumonia, or referral-level danger.

sections.title: Chief complaint
sections.text: Cough for 4 days with fever since yesterday

sections.title: Caregiver concern
sections.text: Mother says breathing seems faster at night but child is still breastfeeding and drinking.

coach.title: Amina arrives coughing and warm
coach.body: You must decide quickly if this is severe respiratory illness or manageable pneumonia.
coach.quote: "She coughs all night and breathes quickly."

teach.label: IMNCI framing
teach.text: In children, age and respiratory rate determine classification. Count breaths before labeling severity.

coach.title: What is the best classification now?
coach.body: Use age-specific fast-breathing cutoffs and danger signs.

question.prompt: For this 2-year-old, what is the safest interpretation?

options.text: Fast breathing pneumonia without danger signs; manage as outpatient and review closely
No pneumonia because oxygen saturation is above 90%
Severe pneumonia needing immediate referral because any fever with cough is severe
Asthma only, so skip IMNCI classification

question.right: Correct. At age 2 years (12-59 months), RR 48/min is fast breathing, and no chest indrawing/stridor/danger signs are documented. IMNCI supports pneumonia management at HC III with close follow-up.
question.wrong: This child meets fast-breathing criteria for age (RR 48/min). Fever plus cough still requires IMNCI classification; oxygen alone does not exclude pneumonia.

sections.title: Management choice
sections.detail: Oral antibiotic per guideline, antipyretic, fluids, and feeding support

sections.title: Respiratory exam
sections.text: No chest indrawing, no stridor at rest, alert, taking fluids.

coach.title: Choose the most appropriate first plan
coach.body: Pick the option that matches findings and avoids overtreatment.

options.text: Start oral pneumonia treatment per IMNCI/UCG, then schedule 2-day follow-up
Give only cough syrup and vitamins because child is playful
Start injectable broad-spectrum antibiotics for all cough with fever
Discharge without counseling because no danger signs are present

question.right: Correct. Child is stable but meets fast-breathing pneumonia criteria. Guideline-based oral treatment and short follow-up reduce progression risk.
question.wrong: RR 48/min at 2 years is not simple cough. Under-treating or skipping follow-up can miss deterioration in the next 24-48 hours.

sections.title: Return immediately if
danger_signs: Breathing becomes difficult or very fast

coach.title: What counseling is essential before discharge?
coach.body: Choose the message that prevents delayed return.

options.text: Explain danger signs clearly and set a strict 2-day review even if slightly improved
Tell caregiver to return only after 1 week if cough remains
Stop antibiotics once fever reduces on day 1
No follow-up needed because pulse oximetry is acceptable

question.right: Correct. For child pneumonia, practical counseling and early review are core IMNCI actions to catch worsening breathing.
question.wrong: A child can worsen quickly. Delayed review or incomplete treatment increases risk of severe disease.

sections.title: Case outcome
sections.text: You correctly identified fast-breathing pneumonia and avoided both undertreatment and unnecessary referral.
sections.emphasis: Age-based RR interpretation changed the decision.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: Amina's RR 48/min at age 2 years meets fast-breathing criteria. With no chest indrawing, stridor, or general danger signs, outpatient pneumonia management with close review is appropriate under IMNCI and Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023.
